tool.name: MahalanobisRaster
tool.summary: Creates a raster of Mahalanobis distances measuring, for every cell, how far that cell's combination of landscape-variable values lies from a multivariate reference mean, scaled by the inverse covariance among the variables.
tool.usage:
The squared Mahalanobis distance for a cell is the quadratic form D2 = (x - mu)' * Sigma^-1 * (x - mu), where x is the cell's vector of landscape-variable values, mu is the mean vector, and Sigma^-1 is the inverse covariance matrix. The reference mean and covariance can be computed from sample point features, from the cells of a categorical raster, or read from previously saved tables.
The computation is performed cell-by-cell (block vectorized) rather than through whole-raster map algebra, so it stays memory-bounded for large rasters and many variables. Predictors are aligned to a common analysis grid; set the Output Coordinate System, Cell Size, Processing Extent, Mask, and Snap Raster environments to control that grid.
Reference: Mahalanobis, P.C. (1936). On the generalised distance in statistics. Proceedings of the National Institute of Sciences of India 2(1):49-55.
Environments: this tool honors the Output Coordinate System, Cell Size, Processing Extent, Snap Raster, and Mask environments. Other geoprocessing environments do not affect it.

dialogReference.para: The raster datasets that define the multivariate space; their cell values are used (never any raster attribute-table values). At least one raster is required - it sets the analysis grid cell size, coordinate system, and extent.
A multiband raster is automatically expanded to one variable per band, named "raster_Band_X". To leave out specific bands, use the Bands to exclude table below.

Order matters: the variables become the columns of the mean vector and covariance matrix in the order listed (rasters first, then polygons), and the same datasets must be supplied in the same order when you reuse a saved mean and covariance (the Existing tables source); a different order silently produces incorrect distances.

Optional polygon variables. Each row is a polygon feature class plus a numeric field, which is rasterized to the analysis grid using that field. Choose the field from the Numeric field dropdown. Polygon variables follow the raster variables in covariance-matrix order.

param.name: exclude_bands
param.displayname: Bands to exclude from multiband rasters (Optional)

dialogReference.para: Optional. To leave out specific bands of a multiband raster, add a row naming the multiband raster and the 1-based band number to exclude. Add one row for each band you want to drop.

How a raster value is read at a location that may not align to a cell center. Exact (nearest cell) uses the value of the cell the location falls in. Interpolated (bilinear) estimates the value from the four nearest cell centers.
This applies when sampling rasters at sample-point locations and when resampling rasters that do not already align to the analysis grid.

Exact cell values are more appropriate for categorical rasters, while bilinear interpolation is more appropriate for continuous rasters. Interpolation is rarely appropriate for categorical data unless the categories are at least ordinal, and preferably interval or ratio; it should never be used for nominal (unordered) categories.

param.name: stats_source
param.displayname: Source of mean vector and covariance matrix

dialogReference.para: Where the reference mean vector and covariance matrix come from.
Calculate directly from sample point features: sample the landscape variables at the supplied points and compute the mean and covariance from those samples.
Categorical raster: compute the mean and covariance from every cell of a categorical raster that equals a chosen value.
Existing tables: read a previously saved mean vector and covariance matrix; the variable order is validated against the tables' stored order.

The reference point features whose locations define the sample used to build the mean and covariance. Points falling outside the extent of any landscape raster, or on a NoData cell, are excluded and reported in the tool messages.
If checked and the points layer has an active selection, only the selected points are used to build the statistics.
A categorical raster whose matching cells define the reference sample. Used only when the statistics source is Categorical raster.

param.name: cat_field
param.displayname: Category field (informational; cell values are used)

dialogReference.para: Informational only - the reference cells are selected by their numeric cell value, not by an attribute-table field.
The categorical raster cell value whose cells form the reference sample for the mean and covariance.
A previously saved mean vector table (written by this tool's optional outputs or the Covariance from Datasets tool). Used only when the statistics source is Existing tables.
A previously saved covariance matrix table. Its stored variable order is used to validate the landscape-variable list. Used only when the statistics source is Existing tables.
How the covariance matrix is inverted to form the inverse covariance.

Standard (inverse): the ordinary matrix inverse. Fast and exact for well-conditioned data and the right choice in almost all cases. It fails if the covariance matrix is singular, which usually means a variable has no variance (all values identical) or two variables are perfectly correlated.

Pseudo-inverse (SVD): the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse computed by singular value decomposition. Use it when variables are strongly collinear or the covariance is near-singular: it returns a stable least-squares inverse instead of failing, though it can mask redundant variables.
The tool reports the covariance condition number; very large values indicate nearly collinear variables.
The output raster of the chosen Mahalanobis value. Defaults to "Mahalanobis" in the current workspace, auto-incremented if that name is already taken.

Which transform of the Mahalanobis quantity to write. All three are functions of the same per-cell squared distance, the traditional Mahalanobis formula D2 = (x - mu)' * Sigma^-1 * (x - mu), where x is the cell's vector of variable values, mu is the mean vector, and Sigma^-1 is the inverse covariance.

Squared distance (D2): the quadratic form itself. This is the quantity traditionally mapped in ecological and habitat Mahalanobis models, and the value required as input by the chi-square typicality transform.
Distance (D): the square root of D2. The literal Mahalanobis distance in the statistical sense, analogous to Euclidean distance.

Chi-square p-value: under multivariate normality D2 follows a chi-square distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of variables. This returns the upper-tail probability that a chi-square value is greater than D2: a 0 to 1 typicality where values near 1 indicate a cell that closely matches the reference conditions.
Check to also write the computed mean vector to a table. When checked, an output name is auto-filled below.

Output table for the mean vector (one row per variable), with the ordered variable list stored in its metadata for later reuse. Auto-named using the raster name plus "_Means"; written only when Generate mean vector table is checked.
Check to also write the computed covariance matrix to a table. When checked, an output name is auto-filled below.

Output table for the covariance matrix, with the ordered variable list stored in its metadata for later reuse. Auto-named using the raster name plus "_Covariance"; written only when Generate covariance matrix table is checked.
Check to also write the inverse covariance matrix to a table. When checked, an output name is auto-filled below.
Output table for the inverse covariance matrix. Auto-named using the raster name plus "_Inv_Covariance"; written only when Generate inverse covariance matrix table is checked.
Check to also write the correlation matrix to a table. When checked, an output name is auto-filled below.
Output table for the correlation matrix, derived from the covariance. Auto-named using the raster name plus "_Correlation"; written only when Generate correlation matrix table is checked.

scriptExample.title: MahalanobisRaster example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: This example calculates a Mahalanobis squared-distance (D2) raster from three rasters currently available in the active map - elev_clip, slope_clip, and curvature - with the mean vector and covariance matrix calculated from a point layer named Sample_Points_for_Mahal, also in the current map. It also saves the four statistics tables. A multiband raster passed as a variable would expand to one variable per band automatically.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\Tools\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") out_gdb = r"C:\Project\Mahalanobis.gdb" arcpy.jenness.MahalanobisRaster( raster_vars="elev_clip;slope_clip;curvature", sample_method="Interpolated (bilinear)", stats_source="Calculate directly from sample point features", points="Sample_Points_for_Mahal", inversion="Standard (inverse)", out_raster=out_gdb + r"\Mahalanobis", out_type="Squared distance (D2): Traditional for ecological modeling", gen_mean=True, save_mean=out_gdb + r"\Mahalanobis_Means", gen_cov=True, save_cov=out_gdb + r"\Mahalanobis_Covariance", gen_invcov=True, save_invcov=out_gdb + r"\Mahalanobis_Inv_Covariance", gen_corr=True, save_corr=out_gdb + r"\Mahalanobis_Correlation")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Creates a raster of Mahalanobis distances from a set of landscape variables and a reference mean and covariance.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Creates a raster in which every cell holds the Mahalanobis distance between that cell's vector of landscape-variable values and a multivariate reference mean, scaled by the inverse covariance matrix of the variables. The reference mean vector and covariance matrix can be computed from sample point features, from the cells of a categorical raster matching a chosen value, or read from previously saved tables. Output may be the squared distance D2 (the traditional ecological-modeling quantity and the chi-square transform input), the distance D (its square root), or a chi-square typicality p-value. Predictor rasters always contribute their cell values, never attribute-table values; polygon variables are rasterized from a chosen numeric field. The distance is computed cell-by-cell with block vectorization for speed and bounded memory on large, many-variable datasets. Method reference: Mahalanobis (1936).
